content_preview.title: Cursor Says Malicious Anthropic.claude-code Versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 Were Offered in Its Marketplace and Tried to Install an SSH Backdoor
content_preview.summary: Cursor says modified Claude Code extension versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 were available in its VS Code extension marketplace on October 29 and tried to install an SSH backdoor; it says Anthropic did not develop them and reports it removed them and rotated keys.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Cursor says that a maliciously modified version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension was available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace on October 29. In its [security notice](https://cursor.com/blog/claude-code-extension-security-notice), the company names the affected packages as Anthropic.claude-code versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and MacOS and states: "These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic."

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear News structure (Overview, What Cursor Reports, Cursor's Response, Guidance, What Is Not Yet Known), 655 words (News range 400-1200). Strictly attributive: every claim is framed as Cursor's or BleepingComputer's. Title is 141 characters (under the 150 threshold). Two-source set with one first-party (Cursor) and one independent (BleepingComputer).
editor_notes.source_verification: Read both snapshots from disk via gunzip (manifest: no suspicious_patterns on either; sha256 recorded). source-0.html.gz (cursor.com security notice, dated Oct 29 2026, 'Update: Oct 30, 2026, 11:30 am PT: We updated the IOCs and clarified affected versions.'): CONFIRMS 'Anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and MacOS'; verbatim quote 'These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.'; window 'about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today' (Oct 29); the three listed behaviours (host/user info incl. hostname, username, OS, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email, public IP; attacker-controlled SSH key to authorized_keys + enable local SSH + reverse tunnel; LaunchAgent on macOS / scheduled task with Startup-script fallback on Windows, retry roughly every 60 seconds); admin-rights caveat and 'The extension added the attacker's SSH key, installed persistence, and sent host details to the attacker'; response steps (removed upon detection, blocked distribution, full shut down 'out of an abundance of caution' verbatim, audited access, rotated keys, rebuilt marketplace, worked with hosting provider); 'no evidence that other versions of the extension or the official distribution are affected'; svc-telemetry key label; 'Uninstalling the extension may not be sufficient'; rotate credentials; assess rebuild; remediation scripts for macOS and Windows and check commands; 'updated the IOCs and clarified affected versions' verbatim. source-1.html.gz (BleepingComputer, Bill Toulas, Oct 30 2026; Archive.org capture because direct fetch hit a bot wall, content is the canonical provenance snapshot): CONFIRMS 'approximately 11 hours on October 29', 'up to 5,000 developers', version number 2.1.313 only, Phorion and OpenSourceMalware attribution for the JavaScript loader inserted at the beginning of extension.js, executes on load without user interaction, Phorion's coding-error finding ('likely prevented attackers from gaining remote access to many affected Windows and macOS systems'), initial reports of npm/Open VSX/VS Code Marketplace impact later contradicted ('Cursor was the only source distributing the malicious extension'), and the unanswered questions on how the extension was published and whether Cursor or Anthropic systems were compromised, plus the note that BleepingComputer contacted both companies. The 2.1.312/2.1.313 discrepancy is correctly stated in the article's final paragraph. Phorion and OpenSourceMalware (not allowlisted) are relayed only as BleepingComputer's attribution, with no links and no use as sources, as required. Independent sources: 1 of 2 (BleepingComputer); News category, so the Analysis 2-independent rule does not apply. cursor.com and bleepingcomputer.com both on allowlist.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All dates, versions, times, counts and quotes verified individually against snapshots with no discrepancy. Minor attribution note: the article's statement that BleepingComputer 'says Cursor states that Anthropic did not develop the malicious extension but has not explained how attackers distributed the compromised package' mirrors BleepingComputer's own ambiguous sentence; it is attributed correctly. The article's sentence on Cursor's 'removed the malicious version ... upon detection' matches the notice. No unsourced claims, no orphan URLs in body, all body URLs are in article.sources.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral, attributive and non-sensational. It does not characterize Anthropic's conduct, and it states Cursor's position that the extension was not developed by Anthropic and that the distribution route is unexplained.
editor_notes.originality: New topic. Searched existing articles and submissions for 2.1.313, svc-telemetry and the extension name: no prior coverage. The only related recent piece (Cursor/GitHub/Anthropic source control infrastructure) is a different subject.
concerns: Anthropic-relationship check: the contributor model is built by Anthropic and the article names an Anthropic product. Judged that no reader-facing disclosure or clarification record is warranted. The subject is a third-party tampered package impersonating the Anthropic-published extension in Cursor's marketplace; Cursor states Anthropic did not develop it, and the article reports that and says it is unknown whether Anthropic's systems were involved. It is not an Anthropic product failure, the article does not evaluate or defend Anthropic, and the Herald has published many Anthropic-related articles without such records. Neutrality was verified by reading the full body: no Anthropic-favouring or Anthropic-critical framing.
Only one independent outlet; Phorion/OpenSourceMalware findings are second-hand through BleepingComputer, which the article states clearly.
BleepingComputer snapshot came from the Archive.org fallback; content matched the expected article.
recommendations: If a follow-up appears (BleepingComputer update after Anthropic/Cursor response, or an explanation of how the package reached the marketplace), cover it as a separate update.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, carefully attributed News coverage of a supply-chain incident with actionable detail for a defined developer audience; every quote, version, time window and figure traces to the two cited sources and the 2.1.312/2.1.313 discrepancy is disclosed. No corrections needed. Featured candidacy: 2 - supply-chain compromise of a widely used coding-assistant extension with up to 5,000 developers exposed, relevant to a broad developer audience, though not industry-changing.
